summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser-based prototype designed to help users explore lunar south pole landing-site conditions through time-based Sun and Earth geometry.

Built with FastAPI and JavaScript, the application integrates NASA/JPL Horizons to retrieve live ephemeris data and calculate the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth from lunar surface observation points. It visualizes their positions relative to the lunar horizon, provides time-aligned comparisons, and generates sampled visibility timelines to help identify potential sunlight and Earth line-of-sight windows. Synthetic demonstration sites and scenarios are also provided to support interactive exploration.

This project addresses the challenge of understanding how landing-site conditions change over time, making complex astronomical data more accessible to mission planners, educators, and the public. Understanding solar illumination and Earth visibility is an important first step toward evaluating potential landing-site suitability, supporting mission planning, and improving awareness of the operational constraints of future lunar exploration.
details:
Project Details

1. What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser-based application that translates lunar astronomical data into interactive visualizations to help users understand environmental conditions at potential lunar landing locations.

The application integrates the NASA/JPL Horizons API to retrieve ephemeris data for the Sun and Earth as observed from the Moon. Using these observations, the backend calculates their apparent azimuth and elevation angles relative to a selected lunar observation point.

The frontend presents these results through interactive visualizations and time-based timelines, allowing users to explore how the Sun and Earth move relative to an idealized local horizon. It also identifies potential sunlight and Earth geometric visibility intervals based on sampled observations.

The application supports both Live Mode, which retrieves real astronomical data, and Synthetic Mode, which provides demonstration scenarios for exploring time-dependent visibility patterns.

2. Benefits and Intended Impact

Lunar landing site evaluation involves understanding changing environmental conditions, particularly solar illumination and Earth visibility.

Our project makes these astronomical relationships easier to understand without requiring users to interpret raw ephemeris data or specialized scientific tools.

Its intended benefits include:

  • Making lunar environmental data more accessible to mission planners, educators, and the general public.
  • Helping users explore time-dependent sunlight and Earth visibility conditions.
  • Providing an interactive foundation for comparing lunar observation scenarios.
  • Supporting early-stage mission planning and educational exploration of lunar surface operations.

Ultimately, we aim to bridge the gap between complex astronomical data and practical, understandable visual information.

3. Tools, Technologies, and Development Environment

The project was developed using the following technologies:

Backend

  • Python 3.11+
  • FastAPI for RESTful API services.
  • Pydantic for data validation and structured data models.
  • HTTPX for communicating with the NASA/JPL Horizons API.

Frontend

  • HTML5 and CSS3 for the user interface.
  • JavaScript for interactive visualizations, data processing, and timeline rendering.

Scientific Data Source

  • NASA/JPL Horizons System API.
  • Sun (NAIF ID: 10) and Earth (NAIF ID: 399) ephemeris data.
  • Moon-centered observation reference (NAIF ID: 301).
  • Geodetic observation coordinates for calculating apparent azimuth and elevation.

Development Environment

  • Python-based backend development.
  • Modern web browsers for application access and visualization.
  • AI-assisted development tools for coding support, debugging, and documentation.

No specialized lunar hardware is required to operate the prototype.

4. Creativity and Innovation

The main creative aspect of this project is transforming astronomical ephemeris information into an intuitive, interactive lunar environment explorer.

Instead of presenting users with raw numerical datasets, the application translates Sun and Earth positions into visual horizon relationships and time-based visibility information.

We also introduced a dual-mode approach:

  • Live Mode: Uses real NASA/JPL Horizons data.
  • Synthetic Mode: Provides controlled demonstration scenarios for exploring different visibility patterns.

This approach allows users to experience the application's core concepts even when working with limited demonstration data, while keeping simulated information distinguishable from actual astronomical observations.

5. Factors Considered During Development

Several important factors guided our development:

  • Scientific data reliability: Prioritized NASA/JPL Horizons as the astronomical data source rather than relying entirely on manually generated coordinates.
  • Time-dependent conditions: Considered that solar illumination and Earth visibility change continuously with observation time.
  • Usability: Designed the application to make scientific information understandable through visual representations rather than raw numerical outputs alone.
  • Technical feasibility: Focused on a lightweight browser-based prototype that could be developed and demonstrated within the hackathon timeframe.
  • Scientific limitations: Current visibility calculations use an idealized geometric horizon. Local terrain elevation, topographic obstruction, and detailed mission-specific constraints have not yet been incorporated.

The current prototype establishes a foundation for future integration of lunar terrain datasets, terrain-aware visibility analysis, solar power estimation, and more detailed communication-window evaluation.
